summary.text: 生 pictures a sprout pushing up from the ground. It is also used for words about birth, being alive, freshness and production; the evidence records these uses but does not establish a single sequence connecting them.

formation.text: An ideographic compound depicting a plant emerging from soil: 屮 is the sprout above 一, the ground mark. Neither is analyzed as phonetic. A later mark beneath the sprout developed into a horizontal stroke, making the base resemble 土.

components.text: The visible component is 屮, depicted above the ground as a sprout. In this graph it contributes to the pictured plant; no phonetic role is proposed.

一 is the ground line beneath the sprout in the early graphic analysis. A later dot was added beneath 屮 and became a horizontal stroke, so the lower part came to resemble 土; 土 is not identified as the original component.

history.text: The curated oracle-bone-style form and the account of early inscriptions show the proposed sprout-over-ground design. The bronze-style form retains this arrangement; the account describes a later dot beneath the sprout becoming a horizontal stroke. These illustrations are modern vector renderings, and the evidence does not provide a dated, artifact-by-artifact sequence.
A later historical dictionary describes plants emerging above soil and glosses 生 as 進, “advance.” The paleographic account treats “advance” as an extended sense rather than the graphic core.

In bronze inscriptions 生 is also reported in a use for 姓, “surname”; one oracle-bone phrase is likewise read as 多生, though 多甥 is offered as an alternative. In this account the whole sign 生 was reused to write a different word because the words were thought to sound alike or similarly. The proposed comparison is modern Mandarin shēng and xìng, and Baxter–Sagart Middle Chinese sraeng and sjengH; these readings alone do not prove the ancient borrowing.

uncertainties.text: The phrase 生月 in oracle-bone inscriptions is interpreted as “following month” in one account; “this month” and other readings have also been proposed. The phrase’s meaning and its relation, if any, to life or growth remain unsettled.

Reported early uses include childbirth, live or fresh animals, and 生月; later examples include living, lifespan, and producing or occurring. The cited examples do not date every token or establish an ordered development among these senses.
The evidence mentions a conservative form 𤯓 and comparisons with other graphs, but does not establish its chronology, ancestry, or a corruption history.

senses.text: 生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this evidence does not establish that childbirth was the character’s first meaning.
生 is reported as an adjective describing live animals in oracle-bone inscriptions. This attested use does not establish its priority relative to the reported childbirth use.
The phrase 生月 is read as “following month” in one interpretation, but other readings are contested; the phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.

Early inscriptions are reported to use 生 adjectivally of fresh or live animals. Separate historical phonology entries also record “fresh, raw”; no chronology connecting this sense to the other meanings is established.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported with the sense “occur” or “produce.” The evidence does not show when or how this use developed from other senses.
A bronze-inscription example is reported with the sense “lifespan.” No transition from the other attested senses is established.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later paleographic interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The supplied evidence does not date this sense or show its development.

senses.period: Warring States manuscripts and later usage
senses.text: A Warring States manuscript example uses 生 for living in opposition to dying. Later lexicographic evidence also records life and living; the evidence does not establish a complete development from the earlier uses.

limitations.text: The inscription examples support several uses but do not establish priority or a securely dated chain among birth, living, freshness, production, lifespan, advance, and life.
The character’s proposed sprout-and-ground image is not, by itself, evidence that every recorded word meaning developed from plant growth.
The “following month” reading of 生月 is disputed and does not demonstrate a semantic transition from growth or life to month terminology.

overview.text: 生 pictures a sprout emerging from the ground. Early inscriptions also use it for childbirth and living things; the evidence does not establish which use came first.

components.text: 屮 is the sprout above the ground line.
一 marks the ground beneath the sprout.
